entities.name: Rhodri ab Owain Gwynedd
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Rhodri ab Owain Gwynedd (died 1195) was a powerful prince of Gwynedd, one of the most prominent medieval Welsh kingdoms, whose turbulent reign from 1175 to 1195 was defined by relentless fratricidal conflict for control of his father's vast inheritance. As a son of Owain Gwynedd, the "Prince of Wales" who died in 1170, Rhodri inherited a fragmented realm constantly challenged by his brothers, most notably Dafydd ab Owain Gwynedd and Maelgwn ab Owain Gwynedd, and by the encroaching power of the English Crown under Henry II and Richard I. His struggle for regional dominance encapsulates the characteristic political instability and dynastic rivalries that shaped 12th-century Wales, preventing a unified Welsh front against Anglo-Norman expansion.

Following Owain Gwynedd's death in 1170, the principality of Gwynedd was plunged into a brutal succession crisis among his numerous sons. Rhodri initially allied with his brother Cynan ab Owain Gwynedd against Dafydd ab Owain Gwynedd, who had seized control of most of Gwynedd. By 1174, Rhodri and Dafydd had imprisoned Cynan, and the following year, Rhodri captured Dafydd, briefly consolidating power over significant portions of Gwynedd. However, Dafydd escaped in 1176, leading to a renewed struggle. Rhodri then ruled over western Gwynedd, specifically Anglesey and parts of Eryri (Snowdonia), from approximately 1175 until his eventual expulsion around 1193 by his nephew, Gruffydd ap Cynan ab Owain Gwynedd.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Rhodri ab Owain Gwynedd's turbulent reign as a prince of Gwynedd exemplifies the intense dynastic rivalries that fragmented medieval Wales, directly contributing to the kingdom's weakness against encroaching English power. His actions and struggles highlight the persistent internal divisions that ultimately hindered the formation of a unified Welsh state.
